If the scheme must keep a positional label: peninitial, not in the strict set, domain ROOT/STEM rather than word. This matches the record's own qv 'set by morphology' and WALS 15A 'Left-edge: first or second'.

sources.quote: Stress, which is important to the distribution of laryngeal contrasts (and ultimately ejective harmony; see Section 4), falls on the second syllable in polysyllabic roots (e.g. bal.k’án ‘horse’, ʒa.ná.wur ‘wolf’; Haspelmath 1995: 64-67). [...] Most affixes are ‘stress-neutral’ (Haspelmath 1995: 67-69). In derived forms involving such affixes, stress falls on the root/stem, and thus either on the first (e.g. hál.tʰ-a ‘meet, imperative’) or the second syllable (e.g. a.qwá.z-u-n ‘to stop’). A smaller number of affixes are ‘stress-attracting’. [...] Given the dominant stress pattern described above and an apparent lack of secondary stress (Zhirkov 1941: 25-30), we analyze the language as having a single foot. sources.quote: 5.3. GENERAL STRESS ASSIGNMENT IN LEZGIAN. The general location of stress placement is on the second syllable in nonmonosyllabic forms. According to Haspelmath (1993), the tendency for stress on the second syllable is so strong that even Russian loanwords are sometimes stressed on the second syllable. For example, Russian karandaš 'pencil' is pronounced as karandaš in Lezgian. Suffixes are either stress-attracting or stress-neutral in Lezgian. The stress-attracting suffixes can usually attach either only to monosyllabic roots (which results in ordinary second-syllable stressed words) or to roots of any length. Most of the stress-attracting suffixes that attach only to monosyllabic roots are plural and ergative suffixes. [...] As for the stress-neutral suffixes, they are almost all inflectional suffixes (e.g. local cases, tense and mood suffixes, etc.).
